design_note: The existing labs cover intersecting privileges and token audience. This sequence adds a hidden data boundary: a cached result may remain stored after the user loses permission. A fresh authorization decision blocks release despite the same principal, tenant and still-valid cache lifetime.

source.title: Authorization Cheat Sheet
source.concept: Validate authorization on every request and deny when required permission is absent. A previously permitted request cannot substitute for the authorization check on a later access.
source.scope: The cache epochs and revocation timing are original application design choices. The scenario assumes a trusted, current permission lookup at every release boundary.

lesson.title: A cache hit does not revive revoked access
lesson.intro: At 10:00, Priya may read order O-481 and ShopAssist caches its result for 10 minutes. At 10:02, her order access is revoked. The next request arrives before cache expiry.

data.invariant: Cache freshness cannot replace current entitlement at release.

read: Principal and tenant are unchanged, so those cache keys alone cannot detect revocation.
The record is only 3 minutes old, within its 10-minute lifetime.
The current permission decision prevents cached content from entering model context.
lesson.question: Does the remaining 7-minute cache lifetime permit returning C-7?
lesson.answer: No. Cache lifetime concerns result reuse, while authorization controls whether this requester may receive it now. The trusted permission check denies release at 10:03. The system may invalidate or retain the stored entry according to its separate cache and retention policies.
lesson.takeaway: Revalidate entitlement when releasing a cached result.
lesson.assumption: Constructed timeline; permission epoch is application metadata, not an OAuth feature. Current authorization is checked before cached data reaches context.
